title: My latest level for Hurricane Harrison, built with AI — Crystal Cavern
author: gravesisme
selftext:
I’ve been building Hurricane Harrison, a bullet-heaven game for iOS, with AI helping across art, code, music, and level design.

This is Crystal Cavern, the newest level I’ve been working on. It’s an active mine in the game’s Underworld where goblins mine power crystals, with rideable mine carts, new enemies, and an optional quest to destroy the mine cart engines.

I’m still experimenting with how far I can take a mostly solo, AI-assisted game project, and I’m learning new things with every level I make.

If anyone wants to try the game, it’s on the App Store. Crystal Cavern is coming in the next update:

https://apps.apple.com/us/app/hurricane-harrison/id6805960242

comments.author: IC_Film
comments.body: How are you making the music? It looks great, really solid!

replies.author: gravesisme
replies.body:
Thanks! I am using Suno for all my music and have been really happy with it for the most part. The final song I end up with for each screen and level ends up an A+ in my opinion, but it might take me a week to get there. 

Since my game revolves around 5 minute runs with a boss monster climax, I try for 6 minute songs, which is the longest it can produce, but anything over 3:30 usually is very suspect and requires using their editing tools to try and extend it or produce a new cover of the sound. 

My last post here was actually exactly about what kind of issues I run into when promoting for instrumental 6 minute songs with no lyrics, which produced a gnarly heavy metal  chorus singing "No lyrics. No lyrics. Instrumentallll" lol  
  https://www.reddit.com/r/aigamedev/s/FrahK3uOYv

replies.author: gravesisme
replies.body:
The art has gone from being 100% code (Phaser originally and Godot now) to a mix of code-generated visuals and AI-generated image assets made through Codex (originally gpt-6.1-sol and now gpt-6-astra typically on medium or high effort).

The main character, Harrison, is based on my real life son and I supplied a reference portrait image of him that was used to generate the initial 4-direction walking sprite sheet, which is the source of truth for the whole game really. Character animation has been particularly challenging because every text-to-image rendering would drift from that source of truth, so I had to develop a Blender-based workflow to establish consistent poses and weapon positions, then use those renders as references for the finished 2D sprites to make sure he looks like the same character no matter which direction you are moving or which weapon you have equipped. 

Level design now starts off with a lot of back and forth with chat-gpt on the look and feel of what I am going for and then identifying the various types of textures, props, structures, and overall flow I am looking for. I then typically hand-draw a rudimentary outline of what I want the level to look like and add small sticky notes that reference the concept art I created with chat-gpt. I then take a picture of that and provide all of the concept art along with a prompt explaining which sticky notes reference which concept art along with some other rules I've established to then create the entire level reference image. From there, I have a fable-5.1 orchestration agent break the level into individual assets and implementation tasks where codex-gpt-6-astra is used for image generation that I have to review and approve before I then have a claude-5.5-opus agent integrate the new assset into the codebase, which I then playtest to make sure it feels natural.

If interested, here is an artifact that was generated during the process of adding 8-direction sword animation where you can see the bottom row identifies where the repaint drifted from the pose, and the pass/fail labels flag frames that needed more correction.

https://preview.redd.it/9f2ho32zbosh1.jpeg?width=2892&format=pjpg&auto=webp&s=a5af989142c085183cf706b84507353d43c6a524
